narrative.what_i_did:
Two operator asks landed this session, both from field-testing on the iPhone. First: the family tree could not actually be edited (the only Name field was the add-a-relative form, so typing a correction minted a brand-new person), it was buried three screens deep behind a modal, and the operator wanted it as its own first-class tab that 'screams delightful info about your Merkle family tree,' with editing that signs each change, a visible history of signed changes, and his governance rule that 'after two signers, both have to sign to change again.' Second, mid-session: the People-tab secrets surface looked cheap (a little paragraph you click to expand), you couldn't see who held your pieces at a glance, bring-back took five screens, and the several secret surfaces felt redundant.

For the family tree I built the correct primitive first. A person-node is content-addressed, so it can never be mutated in place without orphaning its kin edges. personEdit.ts adds an append-only, signed CORRECTION attestation that names the target node and carries a full new snapshot of the editable fields (display name, born, died, sex) or a removal flag. buildKinGraph folds the corrections over each canonical node latest-wins so the tree shows the corrected person, while the whole chain of who-changed-what-when stays on the ledger. The governance rule is real, not decorative: the fold tracks the node's controlling signer set and, once it reaches two, only APPLIES a correction that carries all their signatures; otherwise the correction is held as pending co-signature, shown in history but not reflected on the tree. Because a person you solo-control (the common case today) stays at one signer, your corrections take effect immediately, which is what fixes the rename bug now. I covered it with twelve unit tests plus a buildKinGraph integration test.

On the surface, Family is now its own top-level tab imported EAGERLY per the operator's 'not lazy' instruction, opening straight to the connected tree with a delightful stat band (people, generations, generations back and ahead, ties, oldest year, anchored-to-Bitcoin). Tapping a person opens an inline detail with an Edit panel (rename, dates, mother/father via the sex toggle, remove), the signed-change history with signed-vs-pending badges, their moments, and grow-from-here, all with no modal. I removed the buried 'Edit family tree' trigger from the People tab. To keep FamilyTreeEditor under the 800-line hard limit after these additions I extracted the whole detail view into PersonDetailView.tsx.

For the secrets module I reframed PeopleSecretsSection from a collapse-to-paragraph into a real module surface (icon tile, purpose line) that opens to your secret cards by default. The ledger cards (SecretsLedgerList) are rebuilt to show, right on the surface, who holds each piece as holder chips with a green check once their wallet has acknowledged holding it, a ready/out status pill, and a one-tap 'Bring it back' per card. Bring-back routes to a focused recover screen for that specific secret that lists who to ask for each piece (with an 'Ask over chat' button for Tapit holders) above the paste box. I deliberately left the wallet-recovery cohort as its own distinct flow rather than absorbing it, since it must stay reachable from the locked-out screen and must not be confusable with a casual secret. Both cuts shipped to main with all four gates green and 743 tests passing.
narrative.whats_pending:
The dual-signature governance on family edits is modeled and enforced in the fold, but the live counter-signature transport is the named follow-on: today there is no flow for the other controlling signer to actually add their signature to a correction, so once a node is co-signed by two people a further edit will correctly sit as 'pending' with no way yet to complete it in-app. That lights up when family co-signing/handshake counter-sign lands. Nothing about it is faked; it just isn't reachable end-to-end yet.

On secrets, the honest gap is that 'bring it back in one tap' currently means one tap to the right screen with who-to-ask laid out, not a true auto-return where the holder taps and the piece flies back and the secret reconstructs itself. That auto-return over the network (request-piece envelope plus the holder's encrypted response, reusing the recovery-ceremony plumbing for arbitrary secrets) is the real follow-on the operator's words point at.

Neither cut has had device validation on the iPhone. The operator should open the new Family tab, confirm the stat band reads right, tap a person, rename them and confirm the tree updates and the change shows in history as 'signed,' and try remove. Then open People, confirm the secrets module looks like a real module, that holder chips show, and that a per-card 'Bring it back' lands on the focused recover screen.
narrative.what_you_could_do_better: Nothing surfaced beyond the declared scope. One judgment worth recording: I made the secrets module open-by-default, which means the SecretsDashboard lazy chunk now loads whenever the People tab is viewed, a small perf cost the previous design deliberately avoided by keeping it collapsed. I judged that acceptable because the operator explicitly wanted it to stop looking like a hidden paragraph and to show secrets 'right off the bat,' but if he finds the People tab heavier on load, reverting to collapsed-by-default is a one-line change. Second: I asked a two-part chip question on secrets scope (own tab vs in-People, and how far to merge wallet-recovery) and the operator denied it and re-sent his message, which I read correctly as 'stop asking, just build it well' — the lesson is that his original message already contained the placement answer ('inside that tab like your people is gonna do something') and I should have extracted it rather than asking.
narrative.bigger_picture: Both cuts are the same doctrine showing up twice: a person's verifiable life is a pile of small signed envelopes, and the right way to change anything is never to mutate in place but to lay a newer signed claim on top and let the graph fold them. The family-tree correction model is literally that — content-addressed nodes that accrete signed corrections with a co-signature rule, which is the append-as-decided governance from the Hearth spec made tangible for one family's tree. The secrets module is the other half of the thesis: take Shamir secret sharing, which already exists, and package it so an ordinary person can split a secret among people they trust and see at a glance who holds what and bring it back, without ever understanding the cryptography. Holding the line on keeping wallet-recovery distinct, and on modeling the dual-sign rule honestly rather than shipping a fake version, is the same instinct in both places: the capability has to be REAL and SAFE before it is reachable, because this is sovereignty-grade software where a confident wrong answer costs someone their keys or their inheritance.

feedback_to_appcommander: Two reinforcements for the skeleton. First, the content-addressed-correction pattern used for family edits is a clean, reusable template for 'editing' anything immutable-by-id in an attestation wallet: never mutate, always append a signed snapshot, fold latest-wins, and gate authority on the accreted signer set — it makes the operator's 'after 2 signers both must sign' governance fall out of the data model instead of needing bespoke UI logic. Worth lifting as a doctrine note alongside the append-as-decided language. Second, the operator's denial of my chip question is a useful signal: he had already answered the placement question in his free-form voice message, and asking again cost a round-trip; the lesson is to extract decisions from the operator's own words first and reserve chip questions for genuinely unresolved forks, which is exactly what PFOR-019 intends but is easy to over-apply. Both cuts also re-confirmed the 800-line file-size gate doing its job — it forced the PersonDetailView extraction, which left the code cleaner than a monolithic editor would have.
